10.1.b:
The operation is finished (→ 08 TKA technique), so the first film answers one question: are the components where we aimed them?

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you read alignment on a TKA film?"
- "The **Knee Society** system reads AP and lateral films: α, β on the AP, γ, δ on the lateral."
- "Targets: femur 5–7° valgus to its shaft, tibia **90°** to its axis, so the mechanical axis is neutral."
- "Judge on a **standing long-leg film**, the limb not rotated and the patella facing forward."

### Standard Views and the Knee Society System
Every TKA film is read the same way, so that two visits can be compared.

#### Views
- Take an **AP** and a **lateral** film of every TKA, plus a **Merchant** (skyline) view for the patella
- The coronal angles need a **standing long-leg** film; the patella and lateral views follow in 10.6

#### Knee Society Radiographic Evaluation
- The **Knee Society** radiographic evaluation (1989) is the standard AP and lateral reading for any TKA (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 10.1 · 10.1
- It covers alignment angles, eccentric placement, tibial coverage, a patellar problem list and radiolucent zones
- Few surgeons fill the whole form; most check only for **notching**

### Knee Society Alignment Angles
Four angles describe the two components in two planes, and a fifth adds them up.

| Angle | View | Measures | Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| **α** | AP | femoral component vs femoral shaft | 90° − valgus cut: a 5° cut gives 85° |
| **β** | AP | tibial component vs tibial shaft | 90° |
| **Ω** | AP | total valgus (femur + tibia) | neutral mechanical axis |
| **γ** | lateral | femoral component flexion | near neutral |
| **δ** | lateral | tibial component vs tibial shaft (= slope) | by design (10.4) |

- The lecturer calls α the distal femoral angle and β the proximal tibial angle
- Campbell's form labels the lateral tibial angle **σ**; most texts call it δ
- Each angle is the film version of a cut, so a wrong angle means a wrong cut (→ 08 Bone Cuts)

### Anatomical and Mechanical Axes
The targets make sense only once the two axes of each bone are clear.

#### Native Knee
- The native tibial surface sits in **3° varus**, the femoral surface 9° valgus to the anatomical axis
- The femoral anatomical axis lies 6° from the mechanical axis and 9° from the vertical
[[FIG: Fig 10.2 · 10.1
- So the native femoral angles are **81° and 99°** (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- In the tibia the mechanical and anatomical axes match; the 1–2° difference is ignored

#### Component Targets
- The femoral component sits in **5–7° valgus** to the femoral shaft (Campbell)
- The tibial component sits perpendicular to the tibial mechanical axis
- A tibial component in more than 5° of varus is never accepted

#### Distal Femoral and Proximal Tibial Angles
- The native anatomical LDFA (lateral distal femoral angle) is 81°
- After TKA it reads 83–85°, because the valgus cut is 5–7°
- The Handbook asks for **83°**: the femoral component is not at 90° to the anatomical axis
- The anatomical MPTA (medial proximal tibial angle) should read **90°**, since the tibia is cut square

MEMORY HOOK — the tilted shelf
- The native tibia is a shelf hung 3° low inside; the TKA rehangs it level, and the femur carries the valgus.

### Film Quality
A wrong film gives a wrong angle, so check the film before the knee.
- Judge alignment on a **standing long-leg film**; short films mislead by rotation and short shafts
- Limb **rotation** alters the coronal angles
- So the patella must face forward, with normal overlap of the fibula on the tibia
- Long films and the CT cut for the epicondylar axis are shown in 08 (Preoperative Imaging)

PITFALL — the rotated AP
- External or internal limb rotation fakes varus or valgus on a short knee film.
- Say → "**I measure on a standing long-leg film with the patella forward and normal fibular overlap.**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **α 85 · β 90 · femur 5–7 valgus · tibia never >5 varus · long leg, patella forward**

10.2.t: Component Position on the Lateral View
10.2.b:
The AP shows varus and valgus; the lateral shows flexion, notching and the posterior condyles.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what do you check on the lateral film?"
- "Femoral flexion (γ): neither **extended**, which notches the anterior cortex, nor flexed, which blocks extension."
- "The **posterior condylar offset** is restored: bone removed equals metal replaced."
- "A poor lateral is repeated as a **true lateral**, condyles superimposed."

### Femoral Component in the Sagittal Plane
The femoral component should line up with the femoral shaft, and the entry point decides it (→ 08 Femoral Entry Point).

#### Measuring the Femoral Angle
- The lecturer's theta angle is the Knee Society **γ**: the component should line up with the shaft (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Draw the anatomical axis from two pairs of points ≈10 cm apart, each pair bisected
[[FIG: Fig 10.3 · 10.2
- On the ideal film, the implant sits perpendicular to that axis, with the posterior offset kept (Prof Abdel Karim)

#### Extended and Flexed Components

| Lateral film | Cause | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **Extended** component | entry point too anterior | anterior notching, limited flexion, recurvatum |
| **Flexed** component | entry point too posterior | incomplete extension, fixed flexion deformity |

- The Handbook names the most important lateral finding: the femur must not be **excessively extended**
- An extended component cuts into the anterior cortex: **notching**, a fracture risk

#### Anterior Notching
- A notched femur is a classic risk factor for a supracondylar periprosthetic fracture (Campbell)
- In one review, **30.5%** of these fractures had a notched femur
- Notched cadaver femurs failed at lower loads in bending and torsion
- So avoid manipulation of a notched knee, and consider a **stemmed** femoral component if found at surgery
- But the link is disputed: in **1089** TKAs, 30% were notched, and the only two fractures were in unnotched femurs
- At surgery, a notch shows during the anterior cut, so stop the saw before it exits (Prof Shokry)
- Finish the other cuts, then make the step deliberately with an osteotome or saw
- If a notch is made, a **stemmed** femoral component protects against fracture
- Supracondylar fractures and their treatment → 15 Periprosthetic fractures

### Posterior Condylar Offset
The posterior condyles decide deep flexion, so the lateral film checks that they were rebuilt.

#### Measurement
- Offset is the distance between a tangent to the posterior femoral cortex and the posterior condylar cortex
- The rule is removed = replaced, so compare the pre- and postoperative films (Prof Abdel Karim)
- An alternative is a **ratio** measured from the anterior femoral cortex, which should not change
- The offset figures are in 07 (Posterior Condylar Offset)

#### Effects of Lost Offset
- A larger posterior cut reduces the offset
- Then flexion is limited, the femur impinges on the polyethylene, and the polyethylene wears faster
- The mechanics → 07 Knee anatomy & prosthesis design

#### True Lateral View
- A poor lateral film hides the condyles, so ask for a **true lateral** view
[[FIG: Fig 10.4 · 10.2
- The true lateral in this case showed the **posterior osteophytes** removed and the offset kept
- So the knee reached full flexion (Prof Sherif Khaled)

MEMORY HOOK — the heel of the femur
- The posterior condyle is the femur's heel: shave it and the knee trips over the insert before full flexion.

PITFALL — the rotated lateral film
- Condyles that are not superimposed make both femoral flexion and offset unreliable.
- Say → "**I ask for a true lateral before I judge flexion, offset or notching.**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **γ neutral · extended = notch · flexed = FFD · offset removed = replaced · true lateral**

10.3.b:
Position is only half of it; the components must also fit the bone and face the right way.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you judge fit and rotation?"
- "The tibia is **flush with the cortex**: no overhang, no undersizing; placement central, not eccentric."
- "Overhang irritates a collateral, the patellar tendon or the popliteal structures."
- "Rotation is invisible on plain films, so a painful TKA gets a **CT** (Berger method)."

### Component Fit and Overhang
The tibial tray should sit on cortex, edge to edge.

#### Sizing
- The tibial tray sits **flush with the cortex** (Handbook)
- An undersized tray sinks into cancellous bone, and an oversized one impinges on soft tissue
- AP templating of component width → 08 Templating

#### Overhang
- Overhang is metal on tendon or ligament, so it gives localised pain, not instability

| Overhang | Structure irritated |
|---|---|
| **Coronal** | collateral ligaments |
| **Anterior** | patellar tendon |
| **Posterior** | popliteal structures |

#### Tibial and Femoral Overhang
- Tibial overhang is **completely unacceptable** (Prof Shokry)
- Medial overhang tents the soft tissue, like an osteophyte, and spoils the release
- So motion falls and **arthrofibrosis** follows, despite good cuts and balance
- Femoral overhang is not acceptable either, but it may be tolerated, as less soft tissue rubs on it
- Mediolateral femoral overhang can still irritate a collateral and cause persistent pain

### Placement and Coverage
The form also asks where the components sit and how much bone they cover.
- **Eccentric placement** (medial or lateral, superior or inferior) leads to subluxation and dislocation
- **Tibial surface coverage**, the percentage of the cut surface covered, is a Knee Society item
- In one bilateral case, the right tibia fitted and the left overhung slightly
[[FIG: Fig 10.5 · 10.3
- This is a case for **gender-specific** implants or PSI (patient-specific instruments)

### Component Rotation on Computed Tomography
Plain films cannot show rotation, so CT measures it against fixed bony landmarks.

#### Indication
- **Rotation** is not seen on plain films, so it needs a **CT**
- Unexplained pain or patellar maltracking with normal films is the usual indication (→ 16 Knee problems)

#### Femoral Component
- Femoral rotation is read against the **surgical epicondylar axis** (Berger)
- This axis joins the lateral epicondylar prominence to the sulcus of the medial epicondyle
- The native posterior condylar line lies in **3.5°** of internal rotation to it in men, 0.3° in women
- The component's posterior condylar axis should be parallel or slightly externally rotated to the epicondylar axis (Miller)

#### Tibial Component
- Tibial rotation is read against the **tibial tubercle** on the same CT
- The tray axis should point to the **medial third of the tibial tubercle** (Miller)

#### Combined Rotation
- Femoral plus tibial rotation gives the combined rotation
- The more combined internal rotation, the worse the patellofemoral problem (Berger)

| Combined internal rotation | Patellofemoral result |
|---|---|
| **1–4°** | lateral tracking and patellar tilt |
| **3–8°** | patellar subluxation |
| **7–17°** | early dislocation or late patellar component failure |
| Well-functioning knees | combined external rotation, 10–0° |

- So CT tells whether one or both components need revision

#### Clinical Effects
- Femoral internal rotation causes flexion-gap imbalance and lateral patellar tilt
- Maltracking and its treatment → 16 Knee problems

MEMORY HOOK — the compass
- CT is the knee's compass: the epicondyles are north for the femur, the tubercle is north for the tibia.

PITFALL — pain with a "perfect" film
- Plain films cannot show component rotation, and internal rotation is a classic hidden cause.
- Say → "**Painful TKA with normal films → CT for femoral and tibial rotation.**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Flush, no overhang · CT: epicondyles and tubercle · combined IR 1–4 tilt, 3–8 sublux, 7–17 dislocate**

10.4.b:
The lateral film also shows the tibial cut in the sagittal plane: the slope.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you measure tibial slope on the film?"
- "Draw a line along the **anterior tibial cortex**, then its perpendicular; slope is the angle to the articular line."
- "Native average **7–10°**; the target is set by the design: PS cut at 90°, CR slope per design."
- "Measure only on a **true lateral**; the proximal 10–15 cm of tibia is enough."

### Definition
Slope is the Knee Society δ angle, read on the lateral film.
- Slope is the angle between the perpendicular to the tibial shaft and the upper tibial surface
- How slope changes the flexion gap → 09 Balancing

### Measurement
Two methods are taught, and both need a good lateral film.

#### JAAOS Method
- Line A runs along the anterior tibial cortex; line B is perpendicular to it (Prof Abdel Karim)
- The articular line passes through 3–4 prominent points, the **anterior tibial corner** included
- Slope is the angle between line B and the articular line
- Typical values are 5°, 7° or 10°, with an average of **7–10°**
- The slope lines on the template are shown in 08 (Posterior Tibial Slope)

#### Handbook Method
- Draw the tibial **anatomical axis** through the middle of the tibia, then its perpendicular
- Slope is the angle between that perpendicular and the tibial articular surface
- The Handbook expects about **7°**

#### Film Requirements
- A long-leg lateral is not needed; the **proximal 10–15 cm** of tibia suffices
- But the film must be a true lateral, with the condyles superimposed

### Target Slope by Design
The right slope is the one the implant was designed for.
- The posterior tilt of the tibial component depends on the articular design (Campbell)
- A PS knee is cut at 90°; a CR knee takes some slope, per its design (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- An advanced extramedullary guide may read, for example, 89°
- A CR knee tolerates more slope than a PS knee
- Slope errors and their results → 08 Posterior Tibial Slope

#### Guide Accuracy
- In cadavers, an **anterior tibial crest** reference gave 3.2° varus to 2.1° valgus (Campbell)
- It also gave a consistent posterior slope
- An **intramedullary** guide was less accurate than an extramedullary one for posterior slope

#### Identifying the Condyles
- The **medial condyle** has the longer articular surface and projects slightly **lower** (more distal)
- The **lateral condyle** is wider and carries the **sulcus terminalis** notch
- On a rotated film, name each outline first, then judge slope

MEMORY HOOK — the ski slope
- The tibia is a gentle ski slope falling backwards, 7–10° in nature; the implant's design decides the slope you build.

PITFALL — the rotated lateral
- Condyles not superimposed make slope and femoral flexion both unreliable.
- Say → "**I measure slope only on a true lateral with the condyles superimposed.**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Anterior cortex → perpendicular → articular line · native 7–10° · PS 90°, CR per design · true lateral only**

10.5.t: Cement Mantle, Radiolucent Lines and Loosening
10.5.b:
After alignment and fit, the film is read for the interface: cement, lucent lines and movement.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you call a TKA loose on X-ray?"
- "Zones: tibia **7** on the AP and 3 on the lateral, femur **7** on the lateral, patella 5."
- "Cemented: a **complete line ≥2 mm** means loose; an incomplete line <2 mm is common and harmless."
- "Other signs: progression, **migration**, subsidence. Exclude **infection** first."

### Knee Society Zones
Zones give a common language, so serial films can be compared.

#### Zone Layout
- Each developer superimposes the component's silhouette on the form
- The zone figure is in 11 (Knee Society Radiographic Evaluation)

| Component (view) | Zones | Layout |
|---|---|---|
| **Tibia (AP)** | 7 | 1–2 medial plateau · 3–4 lateral · 5–7 medial stem, tip, lateral stem |
| **Tibia (lateral)** | 3 | 1 anterior · 2 posterior · 3 stem tip |
| **Femur (lateral)** | 7 | 1–2 anterior flange · 3–4 posterior condyle · 5–7 chamfers and peg |
| **Patella (axial)** | 5 | 1–2 edges · 3–5 around pegs (3 if one peg) |

#### The Handbook's Version
- The Handbook numbers the tibia medial to lateral: zones 1–4 across the plateaus, 5–7 around the stem
- For a CR femur, it runs front to back: 1 flange, 2 anterior chamfer, 3 posterior chamfer, 4 posterior condyle
- Its zones 5–7 sit around the pegs, 7 behind the central peg
- It adds that the zones change with the component's shape, with or without a box
- The book keeps Campbell's form, because the exam form is the Knee Society one

#### Scoring
- The lucency depth in each zone is measured in millimetres and summed per component (Campbell)
- The score thresholds (≤4, 5–9, ≥10) → 11 Radiolucency and loosening criteria
- A stable thin line is common; **widening** or spread on serial films means loosening

### Radiographic Signs of Loosening
A line alone is not loosening; its width, completeness and change decide.

#### Cemented Components
- A complete line of **≥2 mm** at the bone–cement interface means aseptic loosening (Campbell)
- An incomplete line of **<2 mm** is common and not linked with a poor outcome
- The loose tibia and the subsided femur are shown in 14 (Aseptic Loosening after TKA)

#### Uncemented Components
- Lucent lines mean there is no bone ingrowth
- Extensive, progressive or painful lines → consider loosening

#### Migration
- **Migration** or subsidence on sequential films means a loose component
- A tilted stem with a periosteal reaction says the same (Miller)
- The insert is radiolucent, so asymmetric narrowing of the metal-to-metal gap means wear (→ 07)
[[FIG: Fig 10.6 · 10.5

#### Infection First
- Progressive lucency with pain means infection until proved otherwise
- So check CRP, ESR and aspiration first (→ 12 Periprosthetic joint infection)

MEMORY HOOK — the crack in the grout
- A loose tibia is a tile ringed by cracked grout: a broken line is cosmetic, a full 2 mm ring rocks.

### Imaging Beyond the Standard Film
Some lines hide behind metal, so the view must be changed, not just repeated.
- Just **4°** of knee flexion hides a line under a metal-backed tray (Campbell)
- So take identical views at each visit
- **Fluoroscopy** sets the beam parallel to the implant surfaces and shows hidden lucencies in unexplained pain
- **CT with 3D reconstruction** shows loosening, defect size and fracture extent despite artefact (Prof Abdel Karim)

PITFALL — lucency is not always aseptic
- A progressive line in a painful knee may be infection, not wear or loosening.
- Say → "**Progressive lucency + pain → CRP, ESR, aspiration before calling it aseptic.**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **7–3–7–5 zones · complete 2 mm = loose · 4° flexion hides it · infection first**

10.5.1.b:
Zones give a common language, so serial films can be compared.

#### Zone Layout
- Each developer superimposes the component's silhouette on the form
- The zone figure is in 11 (Knee Society Radiographic Evaluation)

| Component (view) | Zones | Layout |
|---|---|---|
| **Tibia (AP)** | 7 | 1–2 medial plateau · 3–4 lateral · 5–7 medial stem, tip, lateral stem |
| **Tibia (lateral)** | 3 | 1 anterior · 2 posterior · 3 stem tip |
| **Femur (lateral)** | 7 | 1–2 anterior flange · 3–4 posterior condyle · 5–7 chamfers and peg |
| **Patella (axial)** | 5 | 1–2 edges · 3–5 around pegs (3 if one peg) |

#### The Handbook's Version
- The Handbook numbers the tibia medial to lateral: zones 1–4 across the plateaus, 5–7 around the stem
- For a CR femur, it runs front to back: 1 flange, 2 anterior chamfer, 3 posterior chamfer, 4 posterior condyle
- Its zones 5–7 sit around the pegs, 7 behind the central peg
- It adds that the zones change with the component's shape, with or without a box
- The book keeps Campbell's form, because the exam form is the Knee Society one

#### Scoring
- The lucency depth in each zone is measured in millimetres and summed per component (Campbell)
- The score thresholds (≤4, 5–9, ≥10) → 11 Radiolucency and loosening criteria
- A stable thin line is common; **widening** or spread on serial films means loosening

10.6.b:
The last part of the reading is the patella: its button, its height and its tracking.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what do you check for the patella after TKA?"
- "Lateral: **height** (Insall–Salvati, Blackburne–Peel), fracture, and a joint line not raised."
- "**Merchant** (skyline): tilt, subluxation and button position. Lateral tilt means **maltracking**."
- "Maltracking makes you think of **component rotation**, so get a CT."

### Patellar Views and Problem List
Two views show the button from the side and from above.
- The **lateral** and **Merchant** views show medialisation or lateralisation, tracking, tilt and button position
- The **skyline** view shows the patella and its tracking
- The Knee Society **patellar problem list** covers angle, placement, subluxation and dislocation
- In one case, the button was centred, correctly rotated and slightly **medial**
[[FIG: Fig 10.7 · 10.6
- A lateral button means trouble

### Joint Line Height on the Film
A raised joint line lowers the patella, so the film checks it against fixed landmarks.

| Landmark | Joint line (Prof Sherif Khaled) | Campbell |
|---|---|---|
| Inferior pole of patella | 10 mm below | — |
| Fibular head | 10–15 mm above | 14 mm |
| Medial epicondyle | 30 mm below | 28 mm |
| Lateral epicondyle | 25 mm below | 23 mm |

- Keep the joint line within **4 mm** of its native level (Campbell)
- A raised line gives patella baja; a lowered one gives instability
- The full rule and the 8 mm lecture limit → 08 Joint Line

### Patellar Height Ratios
Two ratios are used, and they disagree when the joint line moves.

#### Insall–Salvati Ratio
- It is the patellar tendon length divided by the longest patellar length (Miller)
[[FIG: Fig 10.8 · 10.6
- Normal is **1.0**; below 0.8 is baja, above 1.2 is alta
- It ignores the tibia, so it does not change when the joint line rises

#### Blackburne–Peel Ratio
- It is the distance from the plateau line to the lower articular edge, divided by the articular length
- Normal is **0.54–1.06** (Campbell)
- It uses the plateau, so it falls when the joint line rises
- The modified Insall–Salvati ratio and patella baja → 16 Knee problems

### Tilt and Subluxation
The skyline view is where maltracking is seen first.
- Lateral tilt or subluxation on the Merchant view means **maltracking**, so check component rotation
[[FIG: Fig 10.9 · 10.6
- Rotation is measured on CT (10.3)
- Maltracking, baja and patellar fracture → 16 Knee problems

MEMORY HOOK — the ruler that ignores the floor
- Insall–Salvati measures the patella against its own tendon and ignores the floor, so a raised floor (joint line) fools it.

PITFALL — normal Insall–Salvati, low patella
- Joint-line elevation lowers the patella relative to the joint, but Insall–Salvati stays normal.
- Say → "**After TKA I use Blackburne–Peel and the joint-line landmarks, not Insall–Salvati alone.**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Joint line within 4 mm · IS 0.8–1.2 · Blackburne–Peel after TKA · tilt on Merchant = rotation**
